title: The Most Useful New AI Features and Tools to Try
dek: A features-and-tools week: Claude gets a browser, ChatGPT learns to move between temporary and permanent, Gemini transcription starts capturing intent instead of just words, and AI video crosses the faster-than-real-time line — all against a headlines backdrop where NVIDIA confirms its $12.9B Hugging Face buy and nearly posts a $100B quarter.

oneIdea.headline: The line between AI assistant and AI operator just got a lot thinner.
oneIdea.summary: No single frontier model dropped this week — instead, a dozen shipped features quietly changed how AI actually gets used. Claude got its own browser, ChatGPT Work got a computer in the cloud, Gemini's new transcription cleans up what you say into what you meant, and video generation now takes less time than watching the result. The quality-of-life upgrades are where AI moves from giving answers to opening the tab and getting the job done — and it's worth taking inventory.

gpCorner.note: AI commentary for UK general practice; not from the podcast

items.title: The scribe is about to be offered an upgrade from writing to doing — that is the line to hold
items.body: Everything in this edition points the same way: the tools are moving from drafting text to opening the tab and acting. Our scribes today write a consultation note that a clinician reads, edits and signs. The next sales conversation will offer something more — code the encounter, order the bloods, generate the referral, message the patient. That is a different regulatory object entirely, and the practice, not the vendor, carries the clinical risk. The workable rule is the one we already use for locums and students: the machine may prepare, a named clinician authorises, and the authorisation is recorded. If Whittemore is right this becomes genuinely useful and the discipline costs little. If Zitron is right the reliability was never there and the discipline is the only thing standing between us and a significant event. Either way the answer to "can it just do it for me" is no, not without a signature.

items.title: Price is the thing to ask about, not capability
items.body: Zitron's sharpest practical point is about billing rather than intelligence: agentic tools consume vastly more compute than dictation, and nobody yet knows what that costs at an unsubsidised price. Practices are being sold AI scribes at a per-clinician monthly figure that is almost certainly below cost while the market is bought. GP partners have seen this film — the loss-leading first contract, the renewal at a very different number, the switching cost by then baked into everyone's workflow. Before signing anything agentic, ask three things: what happens to the price at renewal, whether the notes are exportable in a usable form if we leave, and whether the contract survives the vendor being acquired. The clinical case may well be sound. The procurement case is where a small practice actually gets hurt.

items.title: The cyber-defence letter is the one item here with a real NHS reading
items.body: A hundred-odd companies, including Visa, General Motors and the major cloud providers, warning that AI-enabled attacks will become far more widespread "in the coming months" and naming hospitals explicitly is not hype — it is the same warning our own ICB cyber briefings have been circulating, from an unusual direction. Nothing about it changes what a surgery should do, and that is rather the point: the defences are still multi-factor authentication that is actually enforced, smartcards not shared, backups tested rather than assumed, and staff who know that a convincing email from the ICB may not be from the ICB. Whittemore treats this as urgent; Zitron would say it is a sales pitch for more AI. The controls it implies are worth doing on either reading, because they were worth doing before anyone mentioned AI.

the_other_side.source: Premium: The Hater's Guide To Circular Financing (Part One)
the_other_side.text: Published the same day, Zitron's argument is that the feature wave Whittemore is admiring sits downstream of a financing loop rather than of demand. On his reading NVIDIA's whole strategy is to "create demand for AI compute for its customers" — which is why, he says, it builds its own agentic platform, spends six billion dollars licensing Poolside and hiring away its staff, and is talking about backing Perplexity at a thirty billion dollar valuation. The quarter Whittemore calls a blowout is, to him, the tell: NVIDIA's largest customers "are, for the most part, funded by NVIDIA", and the swelling receivables and the quietly paused neocloud revenue-share programme are what that looks like from the inside. Part one is paywalled beyond the setup, so the readable claim is the structural one — that agentic products exist to justify GPU purchases, rather than GPU purchases following from agentic products people pay for.

the_truth_beneath.text: The single variable both men orbit is whether agentic AI generates genuine end-user demand or manufactured compute demand. Both accept the same facts: NVIDIA booked ninety-six billion dollars, its days sales outstanding moved from forty-five to sixty, it is financing several of its own customers, and a dozen agentic features really did ship this week. The empirical question that will resolve is whether those features convert into revenue customers pay unsubsidised prices for, and the observable that settles it is what happens to usage when token costs are passed through in full. The residue is pure worldview: whether a supplier funding its buyers is ordinary ecosystem investment or a closed loop. Whittemore is vindicated if agentic products retain paying users at real prices; Zitron is vindicated if usage collapses the moment the subsidy is withdrawn. Both are polemicists with incentives — Whittemore bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype — and the signal is where they agree despite opposite priors: the receivables and the paused revenue-share programme matter. Watch the receivables line next quarter.

headlines.headline: NVIDIA buys Hugging Face for $12.9B — at 80× revenue
headlines.summary: The Information broke the story late Wednesday after NVIDIA's earnings call. Hugging Face only has $150M in annualized revenue, so NVIDIA is technically paying around 80× — versus roughly 15× for SpaceX's $60B Cursor acquisition. But NVIDIA isn't buying revenue; it's buying the premier distribution channel for open models.

headlines.headline: NVIDIA is acquiring its way into a full-stack open AI business
headlines.summary: The pattern: a $6B Poolside licensing deal that brought in ~100 veteran AI researchers, a strategic Perplexity partnership for harnesses and app-layer exposure, and NeMo-Tron going from tech demo to real open-model contender in six months. It's also defense — as the biggest chip customers build their own silicon, open models downloaded, fine-tuned, and served on NVIDIA GPUs through CUDA are the counterweight.

headlines.headline: The neutrality question hangs over NVIDIA's Hugging Face
headlines.summary: Hugging Face is valuable partly because it's perceived as independent — its users include researchers, enterprises, cloud providers, and NVIDIA's own competitors. Eric Hartford calls the deal a loss for open source and 'an opportunity for a new standard bearer to arise.' Still, there's notably more optimism around this acquisition than usual — a sign of how much trust NVIDIA has built in the AI community.

headlines.headline: NVIDIA blows the doors off: $96.2B quarter, 106% growth
headlines.summary: Revenue growth accelerated 21 points over Q1, tantalizingly close to the $100B/quarter milestone only five other companies have hit. Guidance cools slightly — 89.5% for Q3 and 70% for fiscal 2027 on supply-chain snarls — but Amazon's new order for two million additional chips (total annual NVIDIA volume is believed under ten million) keeps demand solid for years. Stock up 4.8% after hours.

headlines.headline: The red flag in the blowout: big customers asking for more time to pay
headlines.summary: Free cash flow fell 50% to $21B while accounts receivable rose 50%, with days sales outstanding jumping from 45 to 60 — NVIDIA cites 'extended payment terms on large multi-quarter agreements with certain investment-grade customers.' Also disclosed: NVIDIA is officially back in China with H200 sales, though well short of what the administration permits.

headlines.headline: NVIDIA pauses its neocloud revenue-share program
headlines.summary: Per the Wall Street Journal, the two-month-old program offering credit support in exchange for a cut of customer profits is on hold after employees flagged antitrust risk and sensitivities about how much control NVIDIA would exert over customer businesses. NVIDIA denies the reporting, saying the model 'is still in place and continues to evolve due to high demand.'

headlines.headline: Salesforce leads the SaaS comeback — stock up 22% in a day
headlines.summary: Agentforce is on track for $1.5B in revenue this year, up from a $1.2B forecast, and Salesforce is now just 5% from filling the entire SaaSpocalypse drawdown. Benioff's victory lap: seats grew across sales, service, and Slack, attrition near record lows, bookings more than doubled quarter over quarter, and agentic platform use surged sixfold. David Sacks: the 'SaaS is dead' narrative is 'getting shredded.'

headlines.headline: The app layer is tripling across the board
headlines.summary: Per The Information: Cognition hit $900M annualized revenue (more than 3× since January), Higgsfield tripled to $700M, Perplexity tripled to $750M, OpenEvidence doubled to $300M, and Manus — even after the messy Meta unwind — claims $400M, quadrupled from last year. DeepSeek's $70M this year is a 10× jump on its full 2025 numbers.

headlines.headline: The FINRA-for-AI executive order stalls out
headlines.summary: A drafted EO would have created an industry self-regulatory body modeled on FINRA — the idea Demis Hassabis proposed in July and Treasury Secretary Bessent publicly backed — requiring labs to share security notes, safety-test new models, and write industry rules. Reported opposition from David Sacks appears to have helped stall it. For now, no FINRA for AI.

headlines.headline: A horrible idea and a Trojan horse for an open source model ban.
headlines.attribution: David Sacks, former White House AI czar, on FINRA for AI (All In podcast)
headlines.summary: Sacks argues that once the body exists, frontier labs will push for standards that apply equally to all models — standards open-model developers would find impossible to meet. He also notes FINRA's reputation among fintech startups: regulation that protects incumbents rather than promoting competition.

headlines.headline: OpenAI, Anthropic, and 100+ companies declare a cyber-defense emergency
headlines.summary: An open letter — signed by Visa, General Motors, and PwC alongside Google, Microsoft, and AWS — warns that AI-enabled cyberattacks will become far more widespread 'in the coming months,' putting hospitals, water treatment plants, and internet infrastructure at risk. It calls for defenders to get better AI tools and cross-industry coordination during a closing 'defender's window.' Ethan Mollick's warning: your organization isn't spending enough before open-weights frontier-class models and harnesses arrive.

headlines.headline: We are happy if you want to work with us or any of our competitors or partners, but please take this moment seriously.
headlines.attribution: Sam Altman, on the industry cyber-defense open letter
headlines.summary: Altman positioned security above competition in his response to the open letter: 'This is a critically important moment for cyber defense with AI. There is not much time to act... Only an urgent and intense collective response will work.'

headlines.headline: Claude Cowork gets a built-in browser
headlines.summary: If a task touches a website — filling out a form, working a web app, agentic browsing — a browser window now opens alongside your session for Claude to use. Nothing to install: it's built into the desktop app as Claude's own sandboxed browser, separate from your logins, with Claude-in-Chrome still there for those who prefer their own.

headlines.headline: In one month, AI went from writing text to browsing the web on your behalf
headlines.summary: With Claude's browser, ChatGPT Work, and Grokbot all landing close together, the small updates add up to a meaningful inflection: AI that gives answers is becoming AI that opens the tab and gets the job done. a16z's Martin Casado draws the distinction sharply — ChatGPT Work is workflow-oriented 'fancy RPA,' while Grokbot, with its own browser and Slack chat, behaves more like a virtual coworker.

headlines.headline: ChatGPT Work's cloud computer gets pitched with... life tasks
headlines.summary: OpenAI's own examples for the feature — booking DMV appointments, setting up apartment utilities, comparing insurance policies, saving apartment listings — are strikingly consumer for a product called Work, an interesting wrinkle in the ongoing AI-for-life vs. AI-for-work divide. OpenAI's Romain Huet: 'ChatGPT Work now has its own computer in the cloud... the possibilities start to feel almost limitless.'

headlines.headline: Temporary chats grow up
headlines.summary: ChatGPT temporary chats can now be personalized with your existing memories, custom instructions, and plugins — and upgraded to saved history when they turn out to be worth keeping. Privacy-conscious users can default to temporary mode without giving up context.

headlines.headline: Finally: multiple Gmail accounts in plugins
headlines.summary: A small update that punches way above its weight — power users juggling half a dozen inboxes have wanted this forever. Claire Vo recently called unconstrained connectors her favorite feature of the new Grok; as NLW puts it, 'I don't care who did it first as long as they all do it.'

headlines.headline: Hermes: the open-source agent copying every big-lab feature within days
headlines.summary: This week: real-profile browsing, where the agent acts with your logins from a managed copy of your Chrome profile. That follows Bot Mode — named specialist bots with their own roles, models, memories, and skills that can talk to each other — plus a HUD overlay mode. Open source, any provider or model, a few dollars a month instead of two hundred.

headlines.headline: Salesforce and Anthropic launch Claude Force
headlines.summary: A new set of plugins and skills lets Claude agents work the CRM directly — using Salesforce data as context, with agentic actions respecting existing governance guardrails via Salesforce's AI Force harness. Benioff: 'Here the UI is the AI... This is how every business will run.' It even got a new Matthew McConaughey ad.

headlines.headline: The X jokes massively undersell Claude Force
headlines.summary: Yes, 'our TAM is the US economy' lab announces a CRM integration — but Thomas Fanning says the deal made him rethink his priors: labs going through software vendors instead of around them signals that data, embedded workflows, and incumbency remain software's moats. The enterprise people NLW actually spoke to were extremely excited; one shelved plans to build a Salesforce alternative to see if this just does what they wanted.

headlines.headline: Gemini 3.5 Transcribe turns rambles into what you meant to say
headlines.summary: The new speech-to-text model supports 85+ languages and offers verbatim mode or 'smart translate' mode, which strips filler, condenses rambling thoughts, and handles self-corrections — plus custom vocabulary for jargon, noisy-environment performance, up to three speakers, and an API. As NLW notes from constantly toggling Whisperflow's cleanup settings, that cleanup is the genuinely hard part — watch whether Google nails it.

headlines.headline: Grok Voice is resolving 15,000 Starlink support calls a day
headlines.summary: Grok Voice Think Fast 2.0 now tops the Artificial Analysis speech-to-speech index, which measures whether voice agents can reason over what they hear and complete tasks with tools. At Starlink, it's diagnosing hardware issues, shipping replacements, and fulfilling over 3,000 orders a week via voice calls and chat.

headlines.headline: Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash is about control, not just prettier video
headlines.summary: The update lets you extend scenes, specify starting and ending frames, add video input references, upscale favorite takes to 4K, and test ideas quickly in 360p — massively more usability for generating video you can use for real things. It hit #1 in the text-to-video arena, though early testers are split on whether it clearly beats Seedance 2.5.

headlines.headline: H3 Max crosses the faster-than-real-time line for AI video
headlines.summary: Fal's new model claims 3.49 seconds average latency versus 68 for Seedance 2.5 and 26.7 for Gemini Omni Flash — one tester generated a clip in 1.3 seconds for 20 cents. Ethan Mollick: 'A line in AI video was crossed' — it can now create reasonably high-quality video in less time than it takes to watch. Investor Steve Jang sees fully generated, massively multiplayer live visual worlds ahead. You can try it on venice.ai.
